data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The premise that a large service has 'strictly more total internal redundancy' is often meaningless because component-level redundancy does not equate to design redundancy; a large service may have many redundant components but zero redundancy against shared design flaws.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The large service's redundancy strategy specifically includes design diversity (e.g., N-version programming) to mitigate common specification flaws.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The decentralized network suffers from a lack of coordinated updates, leaving nodes with unpatched, divergent flaws that cause a cascade of independent failures indistinguishable from a correlated outage in impact.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The failure mode in question is not a design flaw but a physical component failure, where component-level redundancy is the most effective mitigation.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Resilience to correlated failure requires diversity of problem-solving approaches (design independence), not merely multiplicity of components. A large service with N redundant components might all share a common design specification flaw. In this case, the 'strictly more' redundancy is illusory. A decentralized network, despite having fewer redundant components, might have more design independence, making it more resilient to correlated design flaws. The debate should be reframed from component count to design diversity.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
